## The situation

**Client:** Westbrook Health Partners, an independent multi-site orthopedic and physical therapy group. Twelve clinics, 240 employees, 55 clinicians. Privately held, profitable, and slower every year.

**Why Ajaia is there:** The chief executive, Priya Raman, told her board that patient visits per clinician would rise 20 percent within a year without hiring more clinicians. She has now hired Ajaia to tell her how. She has budget, she has attention, and she has already been pitched three AI platforms by vendors. She wants to know what to do first and what it will be worth.

**Your role:** You ran the discovery week. Below is what you came back with. You have 90 minutes before you have to be useful, and then you are in front of her.

**Systems in play:** an electronic health record system, which is the software that holds patient charts, orders, and scheduling, referred to below as the EHR; roughly a dozen insurance payer portals, one per insurer, used to request approval before certain procedures; Outlook; a shared drive; and a set of spreadsheets the operations team maintains by hand.

**One term you will need.** A prior authorization is the approval an insurer must give before it will pay for a procedure. Staff assemble the patient's clinical information and submit it through that insurer's portal. Every insurer wants it in a different format. Nothing can be scheduled until it comes back.

## The materials

**Artifact A. Discovery call, Dana Reyes, Chief Operating Officer. Transcript excerpt.**

"So the way it is supposed to work is, the clinician sees the patient, documents the visit in the EHR, orders whatever they are ordering, and if it needs prior authorization our auth team picks it up and submits it. Everything lives in the EHR. That is the system of record, that has always been the rule.

In practice, is it always clean? No. Look, our clinicians are clinicians. Some of them close their charts the same day and some of them, I will just say, do not. The high-volume ones have their own way of working and I am not going to break what is working for them.

The bottleneck is definitely prior authorization. It takes forever. My auth team will tell you they spend most of their week typing the same clinical information into eight different payer portals, because every payer wants it in their own format. That is the thing everybody complains about.

Referrals are the other one. A physician in the community sends us a patient, and we should be reaching out within forty-eight hours. Sometimes we do. Sometimes the referral sits, and the patient goes somewhere else, and the referring physician stops sending us anybody. I do not have a number on how often that happens. It happens.

Records requests, that is a volume thing. A patient's attorney needs a chart, another practice needs a chart, disability paperwork, and it is just a grind. High volume, low value. Marcus has the numbers on that one, he has been tracking it."

**Artifact C. Email, Marcus Bell, Chief Financial Officer, to you.**

Subject: numbers you asked for

Here is what I have. Caveat that some of this is estimated and I would not take any of it to a bank.

- Records requests: 1,840 last quarter. Average turnaround 4.2 hours. I pulled that from the request log timestamps.
- Clinicians: 55 across 12 clinics. Average roughly 2,900 patient visits a year each.
- Operations and front office staff: 45, fully loaded cost averages around $71K.
- Prior authorizations: about 1,100 a month across the group. First-pass approval rate is somewhere around 70 percent but I do not fully trust that number, it comes out of the EHR and the EHR only knows what people put in it.
- Inbound referrals: roughly 900 a month. I cannot tell you how many of those turn into a scheduled visit. Nobody has ever connected those two systems.
- Patient no-show rate: 14 percent. That one I do trust, it comes off the schedule.

What I do not have and cannot get you this week: how clinicians actually spend their non-clinical time. Nobody tracks it. When Priya says visits per clinician goes up 20 percent, I genuinely do not know what the denominator is today.

**Artifact D. The operations spreadsheet, described.**

The operations team maintains a workbook called Prior Auth Tracker MASTER v7 FINAL.xlsx on the shared drive. One row per open authorization. Columns are patient initials, clinician, payer, procedure, date submitted, date decision received, status, and a free-text notes column.

It is updated by hand by whoever gets to it. Every piece of information in it also exists in the EHR, and some of it also exists in the payer portals. The three sources disagree often enough that the operations team treats the spreadsheet as the real one, because it is the only place the notes column exists.

Nine people have edit access. Four use it daily.

**Artifact F. Note from Alicia Grant, Compliance and Privacy Officer.**

Two things to be aware of before you propose anything.

First, a licensed clinician has to review and sign anything that goes into the medical record or that constitutes a clinical judgment, including a statement of medical necessity supporting an authorization request. A machine can draft it. A machine cannot be the one who attests to it. That is not a Westbrook policy we can change.

Second, we operate under HIPAA, the federal law governing protected health information. Any vendor whose software touches patient data needs a signed business associate agreement with us before that data goes anywhere near it. I can tell you we have those in place for the EHR and the payer portals. I cannot tell you what else people are using. Nobody has ever asked me that question, and I would like the answer before you put patient information into anything new.

## Your tasks

Five tasks, 90 minutes total. There are no word limits and no slide limits. Length is your judgment and we score it: an executive who has to hunt for your recommendation has not been served, and neither has an engineer handed four pages of context and no acceptance criteria.

Budget the 90 minutes yourself. The deck takes longer than people expect and you will be presenting it, so plan backward from that.

### Task 1. Opportunity triage

Before you rank anything, state the basis you are ranking on. Then apply it to every item, including the last one.

Produce a ranked triage of the opportunities you see in these materials. For each item:

- Name it in one line.
- Tag it: process fix, automation, or AI. Use the tag you actually believe, not the one the client wants to hear.
- Say what evidence in the materials supports it, and what you are assuming.
- Say what it is roughly worth, or say plainly that you cannot size it yet and what you would need to.

Then answer two things directly:

- What would you not touch, and why? Name at least one thing that looks like an opportunity and should be left alone or deferred.
- Where do these materials contradict each other or mislead? Name every conflict you found and say which version you are working from.

### Task 2. Current-state diagram and information gaps

**2A. Diagram.** Pick the single workflow you would attack first and map its current state. Any readable format works: a text flow, Mermaid, numbered steps with owner tags, a table, or an image.

It has to show actors, systems touched, decision points, handoffs between people, and the specific points where the process breaks or leaks. Mark anything you are inferring rather than reading directly from the materials.

**2B. Information gaps.** List the questions you would ask in the next client conversation. For each, say who you would ask, and what changes in your plan depending on the answer. A question that does not change your plan is not worth asking.

### Task 3. The CEO deck

Build the deck you will present to Priya Raman. Submit it as a PDF or PowerPoint file.

This is a real client deliverable and it is scored as one. It has to carry:

- Your recommendation, on slide one. Not context, not a summary of what you found. The recommendation.
- What you actually found, compressed. She lived through the discovery week; do not replay it to her.
- A 90-day sequence, with what happens in what order and why that order.
- What it costs her, in her people's time as well as money.
- The outcome you are committing to, stated as a number, and how it will be measured.
- The baseline you have to capture first, and what happens if nobody captures it.
- The largest risk, and what you would do about it before it lands.
- The single decision you need from her, on the last slide.

Build it so she can decide from it. She is smart, she is busy, she has already been pitched by three vendors, and she will be annoyed if you spend a slide explaining what a large language model is.

### Task 4. The build specification for engineering

Take the single highest-priority item from your triage and write the specification your forward deployed engineering partner works from. Cover:

- The problem, stated as the outcome the system must produce, not as the feature.
- In scope and, explicitly, out of scope.
- Systems and data involved, and what has to be true about that data for this to work at all.
- Where a human stays in the loop, and why that gate exists.
- Acceptance criteria. How the engineer knows it is done, in terms someone could actually test.
- The two or three ways this most likely fails in production, and what you want built to catch each one.
- What you need from the client before day one.
- The condition under which you would kill this and do something else instead.

### Task 5. AI Workflow Note

- Which tools and models you used, and on which task.
- What you deliberately kept human, and why.
- One specific thing you checked, corrected, or rejected from an AI output during this assessment.

## The two videos

Record these after the 90 minutes are up. Put both links at the top of your document. Host them wherever is easiest, including YouTube unlisted. If you use YouTube, put Ajaia in the title or description.

### Video 1. The C-suite presentation. 10 minutes.

Present your deck to Priya Raman and her leadership team as if they are in the room.

Record your screen and yourself at the same time. We need to see the slides and see you presenting them. Most screen recorders do this with a webcam overlay. Zoom, Loom, QuickTime with a camera window, or anything else you already use is fine.

Do not read the slides aloud. Present them. Assume Priya interrupts you around minute two to ask "why not just buy one of the three platforms I have already been pitched?" and answer her.

### Video 2. You. 2 to 3 minutes.

No screen share needed for this one, just you on camera.

- Why this role and why Ajaia.
- What you enjoyed about this exercise, and what you did not.
- Your salary expectations for this role. We ask for expectations only. Do not tell us what you currently earn, and we will not ask.

Be straight with us on the second point. "It was great" tells us nothing, and we would rather hear that a task was badly scoped than have you be polite about it.
